Not that the Sabbath was first instituted at Sinai, as if it were an exclusively Jewish ordinance (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.2">Ge 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>), but it was then more formally enacted, when, owing to the apostasy of the world from the original revelation, one people was called out (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">De 5:15</reference>) to be the covenant-people of God.<div eID="gen20506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctify them--</hi>The observance of the Sabbath contemplated by God was not a mere outward rest, but a spiritual dedication of the day to the glory of God and the good of man. Otherwise it would not be, as it is made, the pledge of universal sanctification (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.13-Exod.31.17">Ex 31:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Is 58:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">14</reference>). Virtually it is said, all sanctity will flourish or decay, according as this ordinance is observed in its full spirituality or not. <div eID="gen20507" type="x-p"/>
entries.faac792ec233434a747ee3bd5dddf9ca95ab2106: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11337"/><div sID="gen20508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11337"/><hi type="bold">13. in the wilderness--</hi>They "rebelled" in the very place where death and terror were on every side and where they depended on My miraculous bounty every moment! <div eID="gen20508" type="x-p"/>
entries.54c987424e90f7afe6b68926445a11953ed42672: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11338"/><div sID="gen20509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11338"/>15. I swore against them (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Psa 95:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.26">106:26</reference>) that I would not permit the generation that came out of Egypt to enter Canaan. <div eID="gen20509" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fd58c5a65f7a78e8849581df930fd370ee91be3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11339"/><div sID="gen20510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11339"/>16. The special reason is stated by Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Nu 13:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.4">14:4</reference>) to be that they, through fear arising from the false report of the spies, wished to return to Egypt; the general reasons are stated here which lay at the root of their rejection of God's grace; namely, contempt of God and His laws, and love of idols.<div eID="gen20510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their heart--</hi>The fault lay in it (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.37">Psa 78:37</reference>). <div eID="gen20511" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e80e3b6e170a788dffd157ce807eb332a43bdd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11340"/><div sID="gen20512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11340"/><hi type="bold">17. Nevertheless--</hi>How marvellous that God should spare such sinners! His everlasting covenant explains it, His long-suffering standing out in striking contrast to their rebellions (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jr 30:11</reference>). <div eID="gen20512" type="x-p"/>
entries.546321e33ff92aba95720d285748f8c28619266e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11341"/><div sID="gen20513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11341"/><hi type="bold">18. I said unto their children--</hi>being unwilling to speak any more to the fathers as being incorrigible.<div eID="gen20513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Walk ye not in ... statutes of ... fathers--</hi>The traditions of the fathers are to be carefully weighed, not indiscriminately followed. He forbids the imitation of not only their gross sins, but even their plausible statutes [Calvin]. <div eID="gen20514" type="x-p"/>
entries.a38002dfcbaa3fc1973f79f2b699e71c5f2527e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11342"/><div sID="gen20515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11342"/>19. It is an indirect denial of God, and a robbing Him of His due, to add man's inventions to His precepts. <div eID="gen20515" type="x-p"/>
entries.a74a16a7a1e1d63a6524cdc68656b57a941db923: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11343"/><div sID="gen20516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11343"/>20. (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.22">Jr 17:22</reference>). <div eID="gen20516" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f200740b6413bad8f03898d9f925737ce5c8261: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11344"/><div sID="gen20517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11344"/>21. Though warned by the judgment on their fathers, the next generation also rebelled against God. The "kindness of Israel's youth and love of her espousals in the wilderness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>) were only comparative (the corruption in later times being more general), and confined to the minority; as a whole, Israel at no time fully served God. The "children" it was that fell into the fearful apostasy on the plains of Moab at the close of the wilderness sojourn (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1">Nu 25:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">De 31:27</reference>). <div eID="gen20517" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad2e0e59d856ff9eef6a91a38c19928273c6b58e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11345"/><div sID="gen20518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11345"/>23. It was to that generation the threat of dispersion was proclaimed (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">De 28:64</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.4">Eze 29:4</reference>). <div eID="gen20518" type="x-p"/>
entries.69a01d448f9787fa2563bec5e7b3c7714e7a4e2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11346"/><div sID="gen20519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11346"/><hi type="bold">25. I gave them ... statutes ... not good--</hi>Since they would not follow My statutes that were good, "I gave them" their own (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.18">Eze 20:18</reference>) and their fathers' "which were not good"; statutes spiritually corrupting, and, finally, as the consequence, destroying them. Righteous retribution (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.12">Psa 81:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">Ho 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Ro 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>). <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference> proves this view to be correct (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.63.17">Is 63:17</reference>). Thus on the plains of Moab (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.18">Nu 25:1-18</reference>), in chastisement for the secret unfaithfulness to God in their hearts, He permitted Baal's worshippers to tempt them to idolatry (the ready success of the tempters, moreover, proving the inward unsoundness of the tempted); and this again ended necessarily in punitive judgments. <div eID="gen20519" type="x-p"/>
entries.c992c0a03ed0568a044dc0f4fcce08d0c65eb6e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11347"/><div sID="gen20520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11347"/><hi type="bold">26. I polluted them--</hi>not directly; "but I judicially gave them up to pollute themselves." A just retribution for their "polluting My sabbaths" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.24">Eze 20:24</reference>). This <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> is explanatory of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.25">Eze 20:25</reference>. Their own sin I made their punishment.<div eID="gen20520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caused to pass through the fire--</hi>Fairbairn translates, "In their presenting (literally, 'the causing to pass over') all their first-born," namely, to the Lord; referring to the command (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Ex 13:12</reference>, Margin, where the very same expression is used). The lustration of children by passing through the fire was a later abomination (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>). The evil here spoken of was the admixture of heathenish practices with Jehovah's worship, which made Him regard all as "polluted." Here, "to the Lord" is omitted purposely, to imply, "They kept up the outward service indeed, but I did not own it as done unto Me, since it was mingled with such pollutions." But English Version is supported by the similar phraseology in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>, see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>. They made all their children pass through the fire; but he names the first-born, in aggravation of their guilt; that is, "I had willed that the first-born should be redeemed as being Mine, but they imposed on themselves the cruel rites of offering them to Molech" (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">De 18:10</reference>).<div eID="gen20521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might know ... the Lord--</hi>that they may be compelled to know Me as a powerful Judge, since they were unwilling to know Me as a gracious Father. <div eID="gen20522" type="x-p"/>
entries.255d49afb51b63fa2f08f8d67ef2d66dfd9e7e1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11348"/><div sID="gen20523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11348"/>27-29. The next period, namely, that which followed the settlement in Canaan: the fathers of the generation existing in Ezekiel's time walked in the same steps of apostasy as the generation in the wilderness.<div eID="gen20523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yet in this--</hi>Not content with past rebellions, and not moved with gratitude for God's goodness, "yet in this," still further they rebelled.<div eID="gen20524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemed--</hi>"have insulted me" [Calvin]. Even those who did not sacrifice to heathen gods have offered "their sacrifices" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.28">Eze 20:28</reference>) in forbidden places. <div eID="gen20525" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbd8940063da3213f6a6016003286df1d751c42a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11351"/><div sID="gen20530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11351"/>30. The interrogation implies a strong affirmation, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">Eze 20:4</reference>, "Are ye not polluted ... ? Do ye not commit?" &c. Or, connecting this verse with <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>, "Are ye thus polluted ... and yet (do ye expect that) I shall be inquired of by you?" <div eID="gen20530" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e3b8900bf65ce9a69aab6357cb9f7115bb83d48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11352"/><div sID="gen20531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11352"/><hi type="bold">31. through the fire--</hi>As "the fire" is omitted in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>, Fairbairn represents the generation here referred to (namely, that of Ezekiel's day) as attaining the climax of guilt (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>), in making their children pass through the fire, which that former generation did not. The reason, however, for the omission of "the fire" in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> is, perhaps, that there it is implied the children only "passed through the fire" for purification, whereas here they are actually burnt to death before the idol; and therefore "the fire" is specified in the latter, not in the former case (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.27">2Ki 3:27</reference>). <div eID="gen20531" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce4f53fe767e52a001baae75806eb8d92da64ee3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11353"/><div sID="gen20532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11353"/><hi type="bold">32. We will be as the heathen--</hi>and so escape the odium to which we are exposed, of having a peculiar God and law of our own. "We shall live on better terms with them by having a similar worship. Besides, we get from God nothing but threats and calamities, whereas the heathen, Chaldeans, &c., get riches and power from their idols." How literally God's words here ("that ... shall not be at all") are fulfilled in the modern Jews! Though the Jews seemed so likely (had Ezekiel spoken as an uninspired man) to have blended with the rest of mankind and laid aside their distinctive peculiarities, as was their wish at that time, yet they have remained for eighteen centuries dispersed among all nations and without a home, but still distinct: a standing witness for the truth of the prophecy given so long ago. <div eID="gen20532" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdaf025125fd3a1b5fab15dd9221be3ddb215073: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11354"/><div sID="gen20533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11354"/>33. Here begins the second division of the prophecy. Lest the covenant people should abandon their distinctive hopes and amalgamate with the surrounding heathen, He tells them that, as the wilderness journey from Egypt was made subservient to discipline and also to the taking from among them the rebellious, so a severe discipline (such as the Jews are now for long actually undergoing) should be administered to them during the next exodus for the same purpose (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.38">Eze 20:38</reference>), and so to prepare them for the restored possession of their land (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.14">Ho 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>). This was only partially fulfilled before, and at the return from Babylon: its full and final accomplishment is future.<div eID="gen20533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a mighty hand, ... will I rule over you--</hi>I will assert My right over you in spite of your resistance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.32">Eze 20:32</reference>), as a master would in the case of his slave, and I will not let you be wrested from Me, because of My regard to My covenant. <div eID="gen20534" type="x-p"/>
entries.295011aed0ea3ef165dcf7abef3b7f3d0408d13a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11355"/><div sID="gen20535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11355"/>34. The Jews in exile might think themselves set free from the "rule" of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.33">Eze 20:33</reference>); therefore, He intimates, He will reassert His right over them by chastening judgments, and these, with an ultimate view, not to destroy, but to restore them.<div eID="gen20535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people--</hi>rather, "peoples." <div eID="gen20536" type="x-p"/>
entries.b76ce5e7792e00becb74b5499e6a18fb919f1d3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11356"/><div sID="gen20537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11356"/><hi type="bold">35. wilderness of the people--</hi>rather, "peoples," the various peoples among whom they were to be scattered, and about whom God saith (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.34">Eze 20:34</reference>), "I will bring you out." In contrast to the literal "wilderness of Egypt" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.36">Eze 20:36</reference>), "the wilderness of the peoples" is their spiritual wilderness period of trial, discipline, and purification while exiled among the nations. As the state when they are "brought into the wilderness of the peoples" and that when they were among the peoples "from" which God was to "bring them out" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.34">Eze 20:34</reference>) are distinguished, the wilderness state probably answers partially to the transition period of discipline from the first decree for their restoration by Cyrus to the time of their complete settlement in their land, and the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the temple. But the full and final fulfilment is future; the wilderness state will comprise not only the transition period of their restoration, but the beginning of their occupancy of Palestine, a time in which they shall endure the sorest of all their chastisements, to "purge out the rebels" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.38">Eze 20:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>); and then the remnant (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.3">3</reference>) shall "all serve God in the land" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.40">Eze 20:40</reference>). Thus the wilderness period does not denote locality, but their state intervening between their rejection and future restoration.<div eID="gen20537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead--</hi>bring the matter in debate between us to an issue. Image is from a plaintiff in a law court meeting the defendant "face to face." Appropriate, as God in His dealings acts not arbitrarily, but in most righteous justice (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.9">Jr 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mi 6:2</reference>). <div eID="gen20538" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b5c42220a777341cb29b537e37aab36d1a95a20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11357"/><div sID="gen20539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11357"/>36. (<reference osisRef="Num.14.21-Num.14.29">Nu 14:21-29</reference>). Though God saved them out of Egypt, He afterwards destroyed in the wilderness them that believed not (Jude 5); so, though He brought the exiles out of Babylon, yet their wilderness state of chastening discipline continued even after they were again in Canaan. <div eID="gen20539" type="x-p"/>
entries.7958770045d635f8806275feae5c6ae973cf3f0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11358"/><div sID="gen20540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11358"/><hi type="bold">37. pass under the rod--</hi>metaphor from a shepherd who makes his sheep pass under his rod in counting them (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">Le 27:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.13">Jr 33:13</reference>). Whether you will or not, ye shall be counted as Mine, and so shall be subjected to My chastening discipline (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">Mi 7:14</reference>), with a view to My ultimate saving of the chosen remnant (compare <reference osisRef="John.10.27-John.10.29">Joh 10:27-29</reference>).<div eID="gen20540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bond of ... covenant--</hi>I will constrain you by sore chastisements to submit yourselves to the covenant to which ye are lastingly bound, though now you have cast away God's bond from you. Fulfilled in part, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.8">Ne 9:8</reference>, 26, 32-38; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.1-Neh.10.39">10:1-39</reference>; fully hereafter (Is 54:10-13; 52:1, 2). <div eID="gen20541" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbf24aa7d60954226a8fb994a449a856cec39a9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11359"/><div sID="gen20542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11359"/>38. (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purge out--</hi>or, "separate." Hebrew, barothi, forming a designed alliteration with "berith," the covenant; not a promise of grace, but a threat against those Jews who thought they could in exile escape the observation and "rule" of God.<div eID="gen20543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land of Israel--</hi>Though brought out of the country of their sojourn or exile (Babylon formerly, and the various lands of their exile hereafter) into the literal land of Palestine, even it shall be to them an exile state, "they shall not enter into the land of Israel," that is, the spiritual state of restored favor of God to His covenant people, which shall only be given to the remnant to be saved (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen20544" type="x-p"/>
entries.f481314ce0054e661558c89d854a41fd10f1ad36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11360"/><div sID="gen20545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11360"/>39. Equivalent to, "I would rather have you open idolaters than hypocrites, fancying you can worship Me and yet at the same time serve idols" (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Am 5:21</reference>, 22, 25, 26; compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">1Ki 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.41">2Ki 17:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.15">Re 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen20545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go ye, serve--</hi>This is not a command to serve idols, but a judicial declaration of God's giving up of the half-idol, half-Jehovah worshippers to utter idolatry, if they will not serve Jehovah alone (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.12">Psa 81:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>).<div eID="gen20546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hereafter also--</hi>God anticipates the same apostasy afterwards, as now. <div eID="gen20547" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9197df5417460f406dbd6a986bb80fef436c43b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11361"/><div sID="gen20548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11361"/><hi type="bold">40. For--</hi>Though ye, the rebellious portion, withdraw from My worship, others, even the believing remnant, will succeed after you perish, and will serve Me purely.<div eID="gen20548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in mine holy mountain--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>). Zion, or Moriah, "the height of Israel" (pre-eminent above all mountains because of the manifested presence of God there with Israel), as opposed to their "high places," the worship on which was an abomination to God.<div eID="gen20549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>not merely individuals, such as constitute the elect Church now; but the whole nation, to be followed by the conversion of the Gentile nations (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, "all nations;" <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>).<div eID="gen20550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>rather, "in all your holy things" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen20551" type="x-p"/>
entries.c53636b49dcc67cc3994277d44af8899031175a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11362"/><div sID="gen20552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11362"/><hi type="bold">41. with--</hi>that is, in respect to your sweet savor (literally, "savor of rest," see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.19">Eze 16:19</reference>). Or, I will accept you (your worship) "as a sweet savor" [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">Php 4:18</reference>). God first accepts the person in Messiah, then the offering (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.40">Eze 20:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Ge 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen20552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring ... out from ... people, &c.--</hi>the same words as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.34">Eze 20:34</reference>; but there applied to the bringing forth of the hypocrites, as well as the elect; here restricted to the saved remnant, who alone shall be at last restored literally and spiritually in the fullest sense.<div eID="gen20553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctified in you before ... heathen--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">Jr 33:9</reference>). All the nations will acknowledge My power displayed in restoring you, and so shall be led to seek Me (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.18">Is 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16-Zech.14.19">Zec 14:16-19</reference>). <div eID="gen20554" type="x-p"/>
entries.475adf566f0108d247bf5b991552d4e1cf72db06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11363"/><div sID="gen20555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11363"/><hi type="bold">43. there--</hi>not merely in exile when suffering punishment which makes even reprobates sorry for sin, but when received into favor in your own land.<div eID="gen20555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">Eze 16:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">63</reference>). The humiliation of Judah (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.1-Neh.9.38">Ne 9:1-38</reference>) is a type of the future penitence of the whole nation (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.14">Zec 12:10-14</reference>). God's goodness realized by the sinner is the only thing that leads to true repentance (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.37">Lu 7:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.38">38</reference>). <div eID="gen20556" type="x-p"/>
entries.0599b168e33890dd03070973da12a11a078dcdf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11364"/><div sID="gen20557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11364"/>44. The English Version chapter ought to have ended here, and the twenty-first chapter begun with "Moreover," &c., as in the Hebrew Bible.<div eID="gen20557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for my name's sake--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">Eze 36:22</reference>). Gratuitously; according to My compassion, not your merits. After having commented on this verse, Calvin was laid on his death bed, and his commentary ended. <div eID="gen20558" type="x-p"/>
entries.b549c9a5598c91714583d7689073fb207b07097f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11365"/><div sID="gen20559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11365"/>45-49. An introductory brief description in enigma of the destruction by fire and sword, detailed more explicitly in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.1-Ezek.21.32">Eze 21:1-32</reference>. <div eID="gen20559" type="x-p"/>

entries.88347b8226ad313519d94f1ece28c55a9b84b5c4: <div eID="gen31750" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31753" type="x-p"/> A deputation of the elders of Israel, as usual, in their distress, came to request Ezekiel to ask counsel of God, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>. In reply to this, God commands the prophet to put them in mind of their rebellion and idolatry: In Egypt, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.2-Eze.20.9">Eze 20:2-9</reference>, in the wilderness, vv. 10-27, and in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.28-Eze.20.32">Eze 20:28-32</reference>. Notwithstanding which the Lord most graciously promises to restore them to their own land, after they should be purged from their dross, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.33-Eze.20.44">Eze 20:33-44</reference>. The five last verses of this chapter ought to begin the next, as they are connected with the subject of that chapter, being a prophecy against Jerusalem, which lay to the south of Chaldea, where the prophet then was, and which here and elsewhere is represented under the emblem of a forest doomed to be destroyed by fire, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.45-Eze.20.49">Eze 20:45-49</reference>. <div eID="gen31753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31754" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31755" type="x-p"/> In the seventh year - Of the captivity of Jeconiah, (see <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>), and the seventh of the reign of Zedekiah. <div eID="gen31755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31756" type="x-p"/> The fifth month, the tenth day - That is, according to Abp. Usher, Monday, August 27, A.M. 3411. <div eID="gen31756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31757" type="x-p"/> Certain of the elders of Israel - What these came to inquire about is not known. They were doubtless hypocrites and deceivers, from the manner in which God commands the prophet to treat them. It seems to have been such a deputation of elders as those mentioned <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.14.1">Eze 14:1</reference>.
entries.b18afa35e5be7a240bc7cf9adec99a5584fdaf53: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31758" type="x-p"/> I will not be inquired of by you - I will not hear you. I will have nothing to do with you.
entries.7dbd2e1d08798b590b6075fe82eecb253c245045: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31759" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou judge them - If thou wilt enter into any discussion with them, show them the abomination of their fathers. The whole chapter is a consecutive history of the unfaithfulness ingratitude, rebellion, and idolatry of the Jews, from the earliest times to that day; and vindicates the sentence which God had pronounced against them, and which he was about to execute more fully in delivering them and the city into the hands of the Chaldeans.
entries.9c58d521f95947095886a3e4e2fe68ab800226f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31760" type="x-p"/> I chose Israel - They did not choose me for their God, till I had chosen them to be my people. <div eID="gen31760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31761" type="x-p"/> I lifted up mine hand - I bound myself in a covenant to them to continue to be their God, if they should be faithful, and continue to be my people. Among the Jews the juror lifted up his right hand to heaven; which explains <reference osisRef="Psa.144.8">Psa 144:8</reference> : "Their right hand is a right hand of falsehood." This is a form used in England, Scotland, and Ireland.
entries.17b7e62a0372e430b8df264c367e1b86bff1f4db: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31762" type="x-p"/> To bring them forth of the land of Egypt - When they had been long in a very disgraceful and oppressive bondage. <div eID="gen31762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31763" type="x-p"/> A land that I had espied for them - God represents himself as having gone over different countries in order to find a comfortable residence for these people, whom he considered as his children. <div eID="gen31763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31764" type="x-p"/> Flowing with milk and honey - These were the characteristics of a happy and fruitful country, producing without intense labor all the necessaries and comforts of life. Of the happiest state and happiest place, a fine poet gives the following description: - <div eID="gen31764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31765" type="x-p"/> Ver erat aeternum, placidique tepentibus auris <div eID="gen31765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31766" type="x-p"/> Mulcebant Zephyri natos sine semine flores. <div eID="gen31766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31767" type="x-p"/> Mox etiam fruges tellus inarata ferebat: <div eID="gen31767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31768" type="x-p"/> Nec renovatus ager gravidis canebat aristis. <div eID="gen31768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31769" type="x-p"/> Flumina jam lactis, jam flumina nectaris ibant: <div eID="gen31769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31770" type="x-p"/> Flavaque de viridi stillabant ilice mella. <div eID="gen31770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31771" type="x-p"/> Ovid's Metam. lib. i., 107. <div eID="gen31771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31772" type="x-p"/> On flowers unsown soft Zephyr spreads his wing, <div eID="gen31772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31773" type="x-p"/> And time itself was one eternal spring; <div eID="gen31773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31774" type="x-p"/> Ensuing years the yellow harvest crowned, <div eID="gen31774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31775" type="x-p"/> The bearded blade sprang from the untilled ground, <div eID="gen31775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31776" type="x-p"/> And laden unrenewed the fields were found. <div eID="gen31776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31777" type="x-p"/> Floods were with milk, and floods with nectar filled, <div eID="gen31777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31778" type="x-p"/> And honey from the sweating oaks distilled. <div eID="gen31778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31779" type="x-p"/> In the flourishing state of Judea every mountain was cultivated as well as the valleys. Among the very rocks the vines grew luxuriantly.
entries.e39e00549cb7b32a202c1b3f32906470a45d6755: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31780" type="x-p"/> Cast ye away - the abominations - Put away all your idols; those incentives to idolatry that ye have looked on with delight.
entries.a388325ab1383e1b47a63ead4deb8ec2ca4ba4bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31781" type="x-p"/> They did not - cast away - They continued attached to the idolatry of Egypt; so that, had I consulted my justice only, I should have consumed them even in Egypt itself. This is a circumstance that Moses has not mentioned, namely, their provoking God by their idolatry, after he had sent Moses and Aaron to them in Egypt.
entries.33bd80440e949aea74765654c0be36b05c9225a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31782" type="x-p"/> But I wrought for my name's sake - I bare with them and did not punish them, lest the heathen, who had known my promises made to them, might suppose that I had either broken them through some caprice, or was not able to fulfill them.
entries.e1003a5f15237f3ca8133e7a64096d76650cda6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31783" type="x-p"/> I caused them to go forth - Though greatly oppressed and degraded, they were not willing to leave their house of bondage. I was obliged to force them away.
entries.ee1d96846b794b3d4285c449fe0598973b83063e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31784" type="x-p"/> I gave them my statutes - I showed them what they should do in order to be safe, comfortable, wise, and happy; and what they should avoid in order to be uninjured in body, mind, and possessions. Had they attended to these things, they should have lived by them. They would have been holy, healthy, and happy.
entries.4c534abb53526583579cd7baae02b816f8388d02: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31785" type="x-p"/> I gave them my Sabbaths - The religious observance of the Sabbath was the first statute or command of God to men. This institution was a sign between God and them, to keep them in remembrance of the creation of the world, of the rest that he designed them in Canaan, and of the eternal inheritance among the saints in light. Of these things the Sabbath was a type and pledge.
entries.ad0dd9e24432cb20480671aba57a26f7c0d9fd0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31786" type="x-p"/> But the house of Israel rebelled - They acted in the wilderness just as they had done in Egypt; and he spared them there for the same reason. See <reference osisRef="Eze.20.9">Eze 20:9</reference>.
entries.1a284e11a068cf64d2e7806a5999a8b0f30285b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31787" type="x-p"/> I lifted up my hand - Their provocations in the wilderness were so great, that I vowed never to bring them into the promised land. I did not consume them, but I disinherited them. See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference> (note).
entries.15a76e287313b0e76b5fcb274a4eeb05784ca25c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31788" type="x-p"/> But I said unto their children - These I chose in their fathers' stead; and to them I purposed to give the inheritance which their fathers by disobedience lost.
entries.17e621ff1676d897bc95cf96b3100cb3b1ee4d96: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31789" type="x-p"/> I withdrew mine hand - I had just lifted it up to crush them as in a moment; for they also were idolatrous, and walked in the steps of their fathers.
entries.249f34ac67d9d20f09a954fe56bdf12847886250: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen31789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31790" type="x-p"/> I gave them also statutes that were not good - What a foolish noise has been made about this verse by critics, believers and infidels! How is it that God can be said "to give a people statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they could not live?" I answer, in their sense of the words, God never gave any such, at any time, to any people. Let any man produce an example of this kind if he can; or show even the fragment of such a law, sanctioned by the Most High! The simple meaning of this place and all such places is, that when they had rebelled against the Lord, despised his statutes, and polluted his Sabbaths - in effect cast him off, and given themselves wholly to their idols, then he abandoned them, and they abandoned themselves to the customs and ordinances of the heathen. That this is the meaning of the words, requires no proof to them who are the least acquainted with the genius and idioms of the Hebrew language, in which God is a thousand times said to do, what in the course of his providence or justice he only permits to be done.
entries.5f82173f632fcc82e7d07f5c6e9e4bb8b5356cbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen31790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31791" type="x-p"/> I polluted them in their own gifts - I permitted them to pollute themselves by the offerings which they made to their idols. Causing their children to pass through the fire was one of those pollutions; but, did God ever give them a statute or judgment of this kind? No. He ever inveighs against such things, and they incur his heaviest displeasure and curse. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference> (note).
entries.32033f92f304d17f1511b3bf86b879e043821956: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen31791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31792" type="x-p"/> What is the high place - מה הבמה mah habbamah, "what is the high place?" What is it good for? Its being a high place shows it to be a place of idolatry. I called it במה bamah, to mark it with infamy; but ye continue to frequent it, even while it is called במה bamah, to the present day!
entries.0a5130d1ce23b9202459f1ce56f6e6a38ba63059: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen31792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31793" type="x-p"/> Ye pollute yourselves - This shows the sense in which God says, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>, "I polluted them in their own gifts." They chose to pollute themselves, and I permitted them to do so. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.20.25">Eze 20:25</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Eze.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> (note).
entries.f577fdee46e6b3185e761a360979d6c95b2c5202: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen31793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31794" type="x-p"/> And that which cometh into your mind - Ye wish to be naturalized among idolaters, and make a part of such nations. But this shall not be at all; you shall be preserved as a distinct people. Ye shall not be permitted to mingle yourselves with the people of those countries: even they, idolaters as they are, will despise and reject you. Besides, I will change your place, restore your captivity; yet not in mercy, but in fury poured out; and reserve you for sorer evils, <reference osisRef="Eze.20.34">Eze 20:34</reference>.
entries.5ee31f312c37371b859537d0b85008f622ecc041: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen31794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31795" type="x-p"/> I will bring you into the wilderness of the people - I will bring you out of your captivity, and bring you into your own land which you will find to be a wilderness, the consequence of your crimes. <div eID="gen31795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31796" type="x-p"/> There will I plead with you - There I will be your king, and rule you with a sovereign rule; and the dispensations of my justice and mercy shall either end you or mend you.
entries.3519f1705c4da2dd23e9af9ce006aed1618358d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen31796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31797" type="x-p"/> I will cause you to pass under the rod - This alludes to the custom of tithing the sheep. I take it from the rabbins. The sheep were all penned; and the shepherd stood at the door of the fold, where only one sheep could come out at once. He had in his hand a rod dipped in vermillion; and as they came out, he counted one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine; and as the tenth came out, he marked it with the rod, and said, "This is the tenth;" and that was set apart for the Lord. <div eID="gen31797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31798" type="x-p"/> I wilt bring you into the bond of the covenant - You shall be placed under the same obligations as before, and acknowledge your selves bound; ye shall feel your obligation, and live according to its nature.
entries.86e471ffc207818d9baf8bd0a98fba5a5b90e693: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen31798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31799" type="x-p"/> I will purge out from among you the rebels - The incorrigibly wicked I will destroy; those who will not receive him whom I have appointed for this purpose as the Savior of Israel. And I will gather you who believe out of all the countries where you sojourn, and bring you into your own land; but those of you who will not believe - will not receive the Son of David to reign over you, shall never enter into the land of Israel, but die in your dispersions. This is what the contradicting and blaspheming Jews of the present day have to expect. And thus, both of you shall know that he is Jehovah, fulfilling his threatenings against the one, and his promises to the other.
entries.879ddf0ed0718efb7e9ed35a65c3574dc5720f01: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen31799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31800" type="x-p"/> Go ye, serve ye every one his idols - Thus, God gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they could not live, by thus permitting them to take their own way, serve their gods, and follow the maxims and rites of that abominable worship.
entries.c27df56205ab1229dea435e48ddba91b35bebc05: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen31800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31801" type="x-p"/> For in mine holy mountain - The days shall come in which all true Israelites shall receive Him whom I have sent to be the true sacrifice for the life of the world; and shall bring to Jerusalem - the pure Christian Church, their offerings, which I will there accept, for they will give me thanks for my unspeakable gift.
entries.da1ddd0e974180dc479813888490300a7c1b1123: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen31801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31802" type="x-p"/> And ye shall know - Shall acknowledge that I am Jehovah.
entries.0b2ad109ee1e8a3b9cf6203ceb9347f1217ffc8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen31802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31803" type="x-p"/> And there shall ye remember your ways - Ye shall be ashamed of your past conduct, and of your long opposition to the Gospel of your salvation. <div eID="gen31803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31804" type="x-p"/> These promises may, in a certain limited sense, be applied to the restoration from the Babylonish captivity; but they must have their proper fulfillment when the Jews shall accept Jesus as their Savior, and in consequence be brought back from all their dispersions to their own land.
entries.344a22c6a6a1e50f5b0408ae2b9474110b474aa4: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen31804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31805" type="x-p"/> Set thy face toward the south - Towards Judea, which lay south from Babylon, or Mesopotamia, where the prophet then dwelt. <div eID="gen31805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31806" type="x-p"/> The forest of the south field - The city of Jerusalem, as full of inhabitants as the forest is of trees.
entries.e1060f62ab60b9810bf58464f5f220288638f996: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen31806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31807" type="x-p"/> I will kindle a fire - I will send war, "and it shall devour every green tree," the most eminent and substantial of the inhabitants; and every dry tree, the lowest and meanest also. <div eID="gen31807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31808" type="x-p"/> The flaming flame shall not be quenched - The fierce ravages of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans shall not be stopped till the whole land is ruined. <div eID="gen31808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31809" type="x-p"/> All faces from the south to the north shalt be burned - From the one end of the land to the other there shall be nothing but fear, dismay, terror, and confusion, occasioned by the wide-wasting violence of the Chaldeans. Judea lay in length from north to south.
entries.f6c0def468c004b1198359c5ed94d84644d9cc10: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen31809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31810" type="x-p"/> All flesh - All the people shall see that this war is a judgment of the Lord. <div eID="gen31810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31811" type="x-p"/> It shall not be quenched - Till the whole land shall be utterly ruined.
entries.731b9d5bc9a3fbd091ccec67dc155bbdcb980ec3: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen31811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31812" type="x-p"/> Ah Lord God - O my God, consider my situation; who will believe what I shall say? They put the evil day far from them. <div eID="gen31812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31813" type="x-p"/> Doth he not speak parables? - הלא ממשל משלים הוא halo memashshel meshalim hu, "Is not he a maker of parables?" Is it not his custom to deal in enigmas? His figures are not to be understood; we should not trouble ourselves with them. We are not obliged to fathom his meaning; and perhaps after all it does not refer to us, or will not be accomplished in our time, if it even respect the land. Thus they turned aside what might have done them good, and rejected the counsel of God against themselves. <div eID="gen31813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31814" type="x-p"/> By dividing the word with our neighbor we often lose the benefit both of threatenings and promises. They voluntarily shut their own eyes; and then God, in judgment, sealed them up in darkness.  <chapter eID="Ezek.20"/> <div eID="gen31814" type="x-p"/>

entries.e7883397c51d20026b5fae211a3b84d55bfebdf2: <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1-Ezek.20.4">Eze 20:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen14952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> The date given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference> applies not only to Ezekiel 20, but also to Ezekiel 20-23 (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>); the prophetic utterances in these four chapters being bound together into a group of connected words of God, both by their contents and by the threefold repetition of the expression, “wilt thou judge?” (vid., <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">Eze 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.2">Eze 22:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.36">Eze 23:36</reference>). The formula התשׁפּוט, which is only omitted from the threat of punishment contained in Ezekiel 21, indicates at the same time both the nature and design of these words of God. The prophet is to judge, i.e., to hold up before the people once more their sinful abominations, and to predict the consequent punishment. The circumstance which occasioned this is narrated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>-3. Men of the elders of Israel came to the prophet to inquire of the Lord. The occasion is therefore a similar one to that described in the previous group; for we have already been informed, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.1">Eze 14:1</reference>, that elders had come to the prophet to hear God’s word from him; but they had not gone so far as to inquire. Here, however (Ezekiel 20), they evidently address a question to the prophet, and through him to the Lord; though the nature of their inquiry is not given, and can only be gathered from the answer, which was given to them by the Lord through the prophet. The ground for the following words of God is therefore essentially the same as for those contained in Ezekiel 14-19; and this serves to explain the relation in which the two groups stand to each other, namely, that Ezekiel 20-24 simply contain a further expansion of the reproachful and threatening addresses of Ezekiel 14-19. <div eID="gen14953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14954" type="x-p"/> In Ezekiel 20 the prophet points out to the elders, in the form of a historical survey, how rebellious Israel had been towards the Lord from the very first, even in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5-Ezek.20.9">Eze 20:5-9</reference>) and the desert (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.10-Ezek.20.17">Eze 20:10-17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.18-Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:18-26</reference>), both the older and the later generations, how they had sinned against the Lord their God through their idolatry, and how it was only for His own name’s sake that the Lord had not destroyed them in His anger (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.27-Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:27-31</reference>). And as Israel hath not given up idolatry even in Canaan, the Lord would not suffer Himself to be inquired of by the idolatrous generation, but would refine it by severe judgments among the nations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.32-Ezek.20.38">Eze 20:32-38</reference>), and sanctify it thereby into a people well-pleasing to Him, and would then gather it again out of the dispersion, and bring it into the land promised to the fathers, where it would serve Him with sacrifices and gifts upon His holy mountain (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39-Ezek.20.44">Eze 20:39-44</reference>). This word of God is therefore a more literal repetition of the allegorical description contained in Ezekiel 16. <div eID="gen14954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> Date, occasion, and theme of the discourse which follows. - Eze 20:1. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass in the seventh year, in the fifth (moon), on the tenth of the moon, there came men of the elders of Israel, to inquire of Jehovah, and sat down before me.</hi> Eze 20:2. <hi type="italic">Then the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 20:3. <hi type="italic">Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Have ye come to inquire of me? As I live, if I suffer myself to be inquired of by you, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> Eze 20:4. <hi type="italic">Wilt thou judge them? Wilt thou judge, O son of man? Make known the abominations of their fathers to them.</hi> - If we compare the date given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>, we shall find that this word of God was uttered only eleven months and five days after the one in Ezekiel 8; two years, one month, and five days after the call of Ezekiel to be a prophet (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.2">Eze 1:2</reference>); and two years and five months before the blockading of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>). Consequently it falls almost in the middle of the first section of Ezekiel’s prophetic work. דּרשׁ את , to seek Jehovah, i.e., to ask a revelation from Him. The Lord’s answer in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.3">Eze 20:3</reference> is similar to that in Eze 14:3. Instead of giving a revelation concerning the future, especially with regard to the speedy termination of the penal sufferings, which the elders had, no doubt, come to solicit, the prophet is to judge them, i.e., as the following clause explains, not only in the passage before us, but also in <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.3">Eze 22:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.36">Eze 23:36</reference>, to hold up before them the sins and abominations of Israel. It is in anticipation of the following picture of the apostasy of the nation from time immemorial that the sins of the fathers are mentioned here. “No reply is given to the sinners, but chiding for their sins; and He adds the oath, 'as I live,' that the sentence of refusal may be all the stronger” (Jerome). The question התשׁפּוט, which is repeated with emotion, “gives expression to an impatient wish, that the thing could have been done already” (Hitzig). The interrogative form of address is therefore adopted simply as a more earnest mode of giving expression to the command to go and do the thing. Hence the literal explanation of the word התשׁפּוט is also appended in the form of an imperative (הודיעם). - The prophet is to revert to the sins of the fathers, not merely for the purpose of exhibiting the magnitude of the people’s guilt, but also to hold up before the sinners themselves, the patience and long-suffering which have hitherto been displayed by the Lord.
entries.b77982778265fb823addf2b0c82d83f2b00d9d3f: <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5-Ezek.20.9">Eze 20:5-9</reference> <div eID="gen14955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14956" type="x-p"/> Election of Israel in Egypt. Its resistance to the commandments of God. - Eze 20:5. <hi type="italic">And say to them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, In the day that I chose Israel, and lifted my hand to the seed of Jacob, and made myself known to them in the land of Egypt, and lifted my hand to them, saying, I am Jehovah, your God:</hi> Eze 20:6. <hi type="italic">In that day I lifted my hand to them, to bring them out of the land of Egypt into the land which I sought out for them, which floweth with milk and honey - it is an ornament of all lands:</hi> Eze 20:7. <hi type="italic">And said to them, Cast away every man the abominations of his eyes, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am Jehovah, your God.</hi> Eze 20:8. <hi type="italic">But they were rebellious against me, and would not hearken to me. Not one of them threw away the abominations of his eyes, and they did not forsake the idols of Egypt. Then I thought to pour out my wrath upon them, to accomplish my anger upon them in the midst of the land of Egypt.</hi> Eze 20:9. <hi type="italic">But I did it for my name’s sake, that it might not be profaned before the eyes of the nations, in the midst of which they were, before whose eyes I had made myself known to them, to bring them out of the land of Egypt.</hi> - <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference> form one period. בּיּום בּחרי (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference>) is resumed in בּיּום ההוּא (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>), and the sentence continued. With ואשּׂא the construction with the infinitive passes over into the finite verb. Lifting the hand, sc. to heaven, is a gesture employed in taking an oath (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.6.8">Exo 6:8</reference>). The substance of the oath is introduced by the word לאמר at the close of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference>; but the clause 'ואוּדע וגו (and made myself known) is previously inserted, and then the lifting of the hand mentioned again to indicate the importance of this act of divine grace. The contents of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference> rest upon Exo 6:2., where the Lord makes Himself known to Moses, and through him to the children of Israel, according to the nature involved in the name Jehovah, in which He had not yet revealed Himself to the patriarchs (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>). Both נשׂאתי ידי (I lifted my hand) and אני יהוה are taken from Exo 6:8. The word תּרתּי, from תּוּר, to seek out, explore, also belongs to the Pentateuch (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.1.33">Deu 1:33</reference>); and the same may be said of the description given of Canaan as “a land flowing with milk and honey” (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>, etc.). But צבי, ornament, as an epithet applied to the land of Israel, is first employed by the prophets of the time of the captivity - namely, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.15">Eze 20:15</reference> of this chapter, in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Dan 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Dan 11:16</reference>, Dan 11:41. The election of the Israelites to be the people of Jehovah, contained <hi type="italic">eo ipso</hi> the command to give up the idols of Egypt, although it was at Sinai that the worship of other gods was for the first time expressly prohibited (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.3">Exo 20:3</reference>), and Egyptian idolatry is only mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.17.7">Lev 17:7</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.24.14">Jos 24:14</reference>). Ezekiel calls the idols “abominations of their eyes,” because, “although they were abominable and execrable things, they were looked upon with delight by them” (Rosenmüller). It is true that there is nothing expressly stated in the Pentateuch as to the refusal of the Israelites to obey the command of God, or their unwillingness to give up idolatry in Egypt; but it may be inferred from the statements contained in <reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">Exo 6:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Exo 6:12</reference>, to the effect that the Israelites did not hearken to Moses when he communicated to them the determination of God to lead them out of Egypt, and still more plainly from their relapse into Egyptian idolatry, from the worship of the golden calf at Sinai (Ex 32), and from their repeated desire to return to Egypt while wandering in the desert.<note placement="foot">The remarks of Calvin upon this point are very good. “We do not learn directly from Moses,” he says, “that they had been rebels against God, because they would not throw away their idols and superstitions; but the conjecture is a very probable one, that they had always been so firmly fixed in their abominations as to prevent in a certain way the hand of God from bringing them relief. And assuredly, if they had embraced what Moses promised them in the name of God with promptness of mind, the execution of the promise would have been more prompt and swift. But we may learn that it was their own obtuseness which hindered God from stretching out His hand forthwith and actually fulfilling all that He had promised. It was necessary, indeed, that God should contend with Pharaoh, that His power might be more conspicuously displayed; but the people would not have been so tyrannically afflicted if they had not closed the door of divine mercy.”</note> <div eID="gen14956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14957" type="x-p"/> Nor is there anything said in the Pentateuch concerning the determination of God to pour out His wrath upon the idolatrous people in Egypt. We need not indeed assume on this account that Ezekiel derived his information from some special traditional source, as Vitringa has done <hi type="italic">Observ</hi>V. <hi type="italic">ss.</hi> I. 263), or regard the statement as a revelation made by God to Ezekiel, and through him to us. The words do not disclose to us either a particular fact or a definite decree of God; they simply contain a description of the attitude which God, from His inmost nature, assumes towards sinners who rebel against His holy commandments, and which He displayed both in the declaration made concerning Himself as a zealous, or jealous God, who visits iniquities (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Exo 20:5</reference>), and also in the words addressed to Moses when the people fell into idolatry at Sinai, “Let me alone, that my wrath may wax not against them, and that I may consume them” (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Exo 32:10</reference>). All that God expresses here, His heart must have felt in Egypt towards the people who would not desist from idolatry. For the words themselves, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.8">Eze 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>; Eze 5:13. ואעשׂ (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.9">Eze 20:9</reference>), “but I did it for my name’s sake.” The missing object explaining what He did, namely, abstain from pouring out His wrath, is to be gathered from what follows: “that I might not profane my name.” This would have taken place if God had destroyed Israel by pouring out His wrath; in other words, have allowed them to be destroyed by the Egyptians. The heathen might then have said that Jehovah had been unable to liberate His people from their hand and power (cf. Num 14:16 and <reference osisRef="Exod.32.12">Exo 32:12</reference>). החל is an <hi type="italic">infin. Niphal</hi> of חלל for החל (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.21.4">Lev 21:4</reference>).
entries.420307c388079907177d73896a7b0d483d90dbca: <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.10-Ezek.20.17">Eze 20:10-17</reference> <div eID="gen14957" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Behaviour of Israel in the Desert</title> <div sID="gen14958" type="x-p"/> Eze 20:10. <hi type="italic">And I led them out of the land of Egypt, and brought them into the desert;</hi> Eze 20:11. <hi type="italic">And gave them my statutes, and my rights I made known to them, which man is to do that he may live through them.</hi> Eze 20:12. <hi type="italic">I also gave them my Sabbaths, that they might be for a sign between me and them, that they might now that I Jehovah sanctify them.</hi> Eze 20:13. <hi type="italic">But the house of Israel was rebellious against me in the desert: they did not walk in my statutes, and my rights they rejected, which man is to do, that he may live through them, and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned: Then I thought to pour out my wrath upon them in the desert to destroy them.</hi> Eze 20:14. <hi type="italic">But I did it for my name’s sake, that it might not be profaned before the eyes of the nations, before whose eyes I had led them out.</hi> Eze 20:15. <hi type="italic">I also lifted my hand to them in the desert, not to bring them into the land which I had given (them), which floweth with milk and honey; it is an ornament of all lands,</hi> Eze 20:16. <hi type="italic">Because they rejected my rights, did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths, for their heart went after their idols.</hi> Eze 20:17. <hi type="italic">But my eye looked with pity upon them, so that I did not destroy them, and make an end of them in the desert.</hi> - God gave laws at Sinai to the people whom He had brought out of Egypt, through which they were to be sanctified as His own people, that they might live before God. On <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.11">Eze 20:11</reference> compare <reference osisRef="Deut.30.16">Deu 30:16</reference> and Deu 30:19. <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.12">Eze 20:12</reference> is taken almost word for word from <reference osisRef="Exod.31.13">Exo 31:13</reference>, where God concludes the directions for His worship by urging upon the people in the most solemn manner the observance of His Sabbaths, and thereby pronounces the keeping of the Sabbath the kernel of all divine worship. And as in that passage we are to understand by the Sabbaths the actual weekly Sabbaths, and not the institutions of worship as a whole, so here we must retain the literal signification of the word. It is only of the Sabbath recurring every week, and not of all the fasts, that it could be said it was a sign between Jehovah and Israel. It was a sign, not as a token, that they who observed it were Israelites, as Hitzig supposes, but to know (that they might know) that Jehovah was sanctifying them, namely, by the Sabbath rest - as a refreshing and elevation of the mind, in which Israel was to have a foretaste of that blessed resting from all works to which the people of God was ultimately to attain (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.20.11">Exo 20:11</reference>). It is from this deeper signification of the Sabbath that the prominence given to the Sabbaths here is to be explained, and not from the outward circumstance that in exile, when the sacrificial worship was necessarily suspended, the keeping of the Sabbath as the only bond which united the Israelites, so far as the worship of God was concerned (Hitzig). Historical examples of the rebellion of Israel against the commandments of God in the desert are given in ex. <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:1-6</reference> and Num 25:1-3; and of the desecration of the Sabbath, in ex. <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.27">Eze 16:27</reference> and Num 15:32. For the threat referred to in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.20.13">Eze 20:13</reference></hi>, compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Exo 32:10</reference>; Num 14:11-12. - <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.15">Eze 20:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.16">Eze 20:16</reference> are not a repetition of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.13">Eze 20:13</reference> (Hitzig); nor do they introduce a limitation of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.14">Eze 20:14</reference> (Kliefoth). They simply relate what else God did to put bounds to the rebellion after He had revoked the decree to cut Israel off, at the intercession of Moses (Num 14:11-19). He lifted His hand to the oath (Num 14:21.), that the generation which had come out of Egypt should not come into the land of Canaan, but should die in the wilderness. Therewith He looked with pity upon the people, so that He did not make an end of them by following up the threat with a promise that the children should enter the land. עשׂה כלה, as in Eze 11:13.
entries.08eb35bf360e11daa94b6f6599a1bae9130f5748: <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.18-Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:18-26</reference> <div eID="gen14958" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Generation that Grew Up in the Desert</title> <div sID="gen14959" type="x-p"/> Eze 20:18. <hi type="italic">And I spake to their sons in the desert, Walk not in the statutes of your fathers, and keep not their rights, and do not defile yourselves with their idols.</hi> Eze 20:19. <hi type="italic">I am Jehovah your God; walk in my statutes, and keep my rights, and do them,</hi> Eze 20:20. <hi type="italic">And sanctify my Sabbaths, that they may be for a sign between me and you, that ye may know that I am Jehovah your God.</hi> Eze 20:21. <hi type="italic">But the sons were rebellious against me; they walked not in my statutes, and did not keep my rights, to do them, which man should do that he may live through them; they profaned my Sabbaths. Then I thought to pour out my wrath upon them, to accomplish my anger upon them in the desert.</hi> Eze 20:22. <hi type="italic">But I turned back my hand and did it for my name’s sake, that it might not be profaned before the eyes of the nations, before whose eyes I had them out.</hi> Eze 20:23. <hi type="italic">I also lifted my hand to them in the desert, to scatter them among the nations, and to disperse them in the lands;</hi> Eze 20:24. <hi type="italic">Because they did not my rights, and despised my statutes, profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were after the idols of their fathers.</hi> Eze 20:25. <hi type="italic">And I also gave them statutes, which were not good, and rights, through which they did not live;</hi> Eze 20:26. <hi type="italic">And defiled them in their sacrificial gifts, in that they caused all that openeth the womb to pass through, that I might fill them with horror, that they might know that I am Jehovah.</hi> - The sons acted like their fathers in the wilderness. Historical proofs of this are furnished by the accounts of the Sabbath-breaker (Num 15:32.), of the rebellion of the company of Korah, and of the murmuring of the whole congregation against Moses and Aaron after the destruction of Korah’s company (Num 16 and Num 17:1-13). In the last two cases God threatened that He would destroy the whole congregation (cf. Num 16:21 and Num 17:9-10); and on both occasions the Lord drew back His hand at the intercession of Moses, and his actual intervention (Num 16:22 and Num 17:11.), and did not destroy the whole nation for His name’s sake. The statements in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.20.21">Eze 20:21</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.22">Eze 20:22</reference> rest upon these facts. The words of <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.23">Eze 20:23</reference> concerning the oath of God, that He would scatter the transgressors among the heathen, are also founded upon the Pentateuch, and not upon an independent tradition, or any special revelation from God. Dispersion among the heathen is threatened in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Lev 26:33</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">Deu 28:64</reference>, and there is no force in Kliefoth’s argument that “these threats do not refer to the generation in the wilderness, but to a later age.” For in both chapters the blessings and curses of the law are set before the people who were then in the desert; and there is not a single word to intimate that either blessing or curse would only be fulfilled upon the generations of later times. <div eID="gen14959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14960" type="x-p"/> On the contrary, when Moses addressed to the people assembled before him his last discourse concerning the renewal of the covenant (Deut 29 and 30), he called upon them to enter into the covenant, “which Jehovah maketh with thee <hi type="italic">this day</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">Deu 29:12</reference>), and to keep all the words of this covenant and do them. It is upon this same discourse, in which Moses calls the threatenings of the law אלה, an oath (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.13">Deu 29:13</reference>), that “the lifting of the hand of God to swear,” mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.23">Eze 20:23</reference> of this chapter, is also founded. Moreover, it is not stated in this verse that God lifted His hand to scatter among the heathen the generation which had grown up in the wilderness, and to disperse them in the lands before their entrance into the land promised to the fathers; but simply that He had lifted His hand in the wilderness to threaten the people with dispersion among the heathen, without in any way defining the period of dispersion. In the blessings and threatenings of the law contained in Lev 26 and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deut 28-30</reference>, the nation is regarded as a united whole; so that no distinction is made between the successive generations, for the purpose of announcing this particular blessing or punishment to either one or the other. And Ezekiel acts in precisely the same way. It is true that he distinguishes the generation which came out of Egypt and was sentenced by God to die in the wilderness from the sons, i.e., the generation which grew up in the wilderness; but the latter, or the sons of those who had fallen, the generation which was brought into the land of Canaan, he regards as one with all the successive generations, and embraces the whole under the common name of “fathers” to the generation living in his day (“your fathers” <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.27">Eze 20:27</reference>), as we may clearly see from the turn given to the sentence which describes the apostasy of those who came into the land of Canaan ('עוד זאת ). In thus embracing the generation which grew up in the wilderness and was led into Canaan, along with the generations which followed and lived in Canaan, Ezekiel adheres very closely to the view prevailing in the Pentateuch, where the nation in all its successive generations is regarded as one united whole. The threat of dispersion among the heathen, which the Lord uttered in the wilderness to the sons of those who were not to see the land, is also not mentioned by Ezekiel as one which God designed to execute upon the people who were wandering in the desert at the time. For if he had understood it in this sense, he would have mentioned its non-fulfilment also, and would have added a 'ואעשׂ למען שׁמי וגו, as he has done in the case of the previous threats (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.22">Eze 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.14">Eze 20:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.9">Eze 20:9</reference>). But we do not find this either in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.24">Eze 20:24</reference> or Eze 20:26. The omission of this turn clearly shows that <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.23">Eze 20:23</reference> does not refer to a punishment which God designed to inflict, but did not execute for His name’s sake; but that the dispersion among the heathen, with which the transgressors of His commandments were threatened by God when in the wilderness, is simply mentioned as a proof that even in the wilderness the people, whom God had determined to lead into Canaan, were threatened with that very punishment which had now actually commenced, because rebellious Israel had obstinately resisted the commandments and rights of its God. <div eID="gen14960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14961" type="x-p"/> These remarks are equally applicable to <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.25">Eze 20:25</reference> and Eze 20:26. These verses are not to be restricted to the generation which was born in the wilderness and gathered to its fathers not long after its entrance into Canaan, but refer to their descendants also, that is to say, to the fathers of our prophet’s contemporaries, who were born and had died in Canaan. God gave them statutes which were not good, and rights which did not bring them life. It is perfectly self-evident that we are not to understand by these statutes and rights, which were not good, either the Mosaic commandments of the ceremonial law, as some of the Fathers and earlier Protestant commentators supposed, or the threatenings contained in the law; so that this needs no elaborate proof. The ceremonial commandments given by God were good, and had the promise attached to them, that obedience to them would give life; whilst the threats of punishment contained in the law are never called חקּים and משׁפּטים. Those statutes only are called “not good” the fulfilment of which did not bring life or blessings and salvation. The second clause serves as an explanation of the first. The examples quoted in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> show what the words really mean. The defiling in their sacrificial gifts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>), for example, consisted in their causing that which opened the womb to pass through, i.e., in the sacrifice of the first-born. העביר כּל־פּטר  points back to <reference osisRef="Exod.13.12">Exo 13:12</reference>; only ליהוה, which occurs in that passage, is omitted, because the allusion is not to the commandment given there, but to its perversion into idolatry. This formula is used in the book of Exodus (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>) to denote the dedication of the first-born to Jehovah; but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.13">Eze 20:13</reference> this limitation is introduced, that the first-born of man is to be redeemed. העביר signifies a dedication through fire (= העביר בּאשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:31</reference>), and is adopted in the book of Exodus, where it is joined to ליהוה, in marked opposition to the Canaanitish custom of dedicating children of Moloch by februation in fire (see the comm. on ex. <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.12">Eze 13:12</reference>). The prophet refers to this Canaanitish custom, and cites it as a striking example of the defilement of the Israelites in their sacrificial gifts (טמּא, to make unclean, not to declare unclean, or treat as unclean). That this custom also made its way among the Israelites, is evident from the repeated prohibition against offering children through the fire to Moloch (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>). When, therefore, it is affirmed with regard to a statute so sternly prohibited in the law of God, that Jehovah gave it to the Israelites in the wilderness, the word נתן (give) can only be used in the sense of a judicial sentence, and must not be taken merely as indicating divine permission; in other words, it is to be understood, like <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference> (“God sends them strong delusion”) and <reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Act 7:42</reference> (“God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven”), in the sense of hardening, whereby whoever will not renounce idolatry is so given up to its power, that it draws him deeper and deeper in. This is in perfect keeping with the statement in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference> as the design of God in doing this: “that I might fill them with horror;” i.e., might excite such horror and amazement in their minds, that if possible they might be brought to reflect and to return to Jehovah their God.
entries.f9871e8b789922b0111486e5a86c38d3f72fb2a0: <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.27-Ezek.20.31">Eze 20:27-31</reference> <div eID="gen14961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14962" type="x-p"/> Israel committed these sins in Canaan also, and to this day has not given them up; therefore God will not allow the idolatrous generation to inquire of Him. - Eze 20:27. <hi type="italic">Therefore speak to the house of Israel, O son of man, and say to them, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Still further have your fathers blasphemed me in this, with the faithlessness which they have shown toward me.</hi> Eze 20:28. <hi type="italic">When I had brought them into the land, which I had lifted my hand to give them, then they looked out every high hill and every thickly covered tree, and offered their sacrifices there, and gave their irritating gifts there, and presented the fragrance of their pleasant odour there, and poured out their drink-offerings there.</hi> Eze 20:29. <hi type="italic">And I said to them, What height is that to which ye go? And its name is called Height to this day.</hi> Eze 20:30. <hi type="italic">Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, What? Do ye defile yourselves in the way of your fathers; and go whoring after their abominations;</hi> Eze 20:31. <hi type="italic">And defile yourselves in all your idols to this day, by lifting up your gifts, and causing your sons to pass through the fire; and should I let myself be inquired of by you? As I live, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah, I will not let myself be inquired of by you.</hi> - The לכן in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.27">Eze 20:27</reference> is resumed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.30">Eze 20:30</reference>; and there the answer given by God to the elders, who had come to inquire of Him, is first communicated, after an express declaration of the fact that Israel had continued its idolatry in the most daring manner, even after its entrance into Canaan.
